samples.text:
The bar chart shows the average salary per year of university graduates in six different fields, after one year and after five years of graduation.

Overall, the salaries in all fields were higher after five years than after one year. Computing had the highest salary in both time and fine art had the lowest.

One year after graduation, computing graduates earned $48,000 and engineering graduates earned $45,000. Nursing was $38,000, law was $36,000 and teaching was $33,000. Fine art graduates earn only $22,000.

After five years, computing was still the highest with $78,000. Law increased very much to $70,000, so it become the second highest and it was higher than engineering, which was $66,000. The other fields increased less. Nursing went up to $47,000 and teaching to $42,000, while fine art was $30,000, it is still much lower than the others.

In conclusion, all graduates earn more money after five years, but the increase for computing and law were bigger than for nursing, teaching and fine art.
samples.why: Overview present and figures accurate · key features covered but presented as a list · repetitive linking and vocabulary · tense, agreement and punctuation errors that do not reduce clarity.

samples.text:
The chart compares the average yearly earnings of graduates from six fields of study at two stages of their careers: one year and five years after they graduated.

Overall, salaries rose in every field over this period, with computing graduates earning the most at both stages and fine art graduates the least. The most dramatic growth was seen in law, which moved from fourth to second place.

In the first year after graduation, computing and engineering graduates were the highest earners, receiving $48,000 and $45,000 respectively. Nursing graduates earned $38,000, slightly more than those in law ($36,000) and teaching ($33,000), while fine art graduates received just $22,000.

Five years later, the average salary in computing had risen by $30,000 to $78,000. Law salaries almost doubled to reach $70,000, overtaking engineering, which grew more modestly to $66,000. In comparison, increases in the remaining fields were relatively small: nursing and teaching salaries both went up by $9,000, to $47,000 and $42,000, while the figure for fine art increased to $30,000, remaining the lowest by considerable margin.
samples.why: Clear overview including the key change in ranking · main features well highlighted with accurate comparisons · good cohesion · some less common vocabulary · one minor article slip.

samples.text:
The chart shows the average annual salaries earned by graduates in six disciplines at two points in their careers: one year and five years after graduating.

All six groups saw their earnings rise over the four-year interval, but the scale of the increase varied widely. Computing graduates were the best paid at both stages, while those who had studied fine art consistently earned the least. Law stood out for the speed of its salary growth.

One year after graduation, computing ($48,000) and engineering ($45,000) led the way, with nursing, law and teaching clustered in the thirties ($38,000, $36,000 and $33,000 respectively). Fine art trailed well behind at $22,000.

By the five-year point, the gap between the higher- and lower-paid fields had widened considerably. Computing salaries had climbed to $78,000, and law graduates, whose pay nearly doubled to $70,000, had overtaken engineers, who were earning $66,000. In contrast, the gains for nursing and teaching were comparatively modest, at $9,000 each, bringing their averages to $47,000 and $42,000. Fine art graduates remained at the bottom of the scale, earning $30,000, less than 40% of the figure for computing.
samples.why: Key features skilfully selected, including the widening gap · clear overview · figures used selectively with accurate derived comparisons · fluent cohesion · precise vocabulary · varied, error-free grammar.
